title: Signal Hunters — notes for performance regressions
content:
Purpose:
Quick, pragmatic notes used by the "signal-hunters" rotation for finding the root cause of token-level and tail latency regressions. This doc is intentionally informal — a scratchpad of heuristics, quick checks, and reusable commands that helped us cut mean time to detect/mitigate on several post-release incidents.

Summary of the approach (one-line):
  - Find the symptom, correlate at multiple signal layers, narrow to smallest change set that reproduces, decide whether to revert/fix/mitigate, and capture an actionable hypothesis.

When an alert fires (immediate checklist):
  1) Capture the alert payload: alert_id, route/model, time window, SLO breach magnitude. Paste into a new incident thread.
  2) Quick dashboard triage (5 min): open the triage panel (dash: app/perf-triage). Check:
     - p50/p95/p99 latency by route and model (last 1h vs baseline week).
     - tokens/sec and concurrent requests trend.
     - success/error rate and 429/503 deltas.
     - GPU utilization by host group, memory pressure, and OOMs.
  3) Decide scope: broad (multi-route) vs narrow (single route/model/region).

PromQL / SQL quick queries we use in the rotation:
  - Prometheus (latency heat):
    avg_over_time(histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(inference_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))[1h:5m])
  - Simple traffic shift:
    sum(rate(requests_total{route=~"/chat.*"}[5m])) by (model,region)
  - Token path hotspots (approx):
    sum(rate(token_generation_steps_total[5m])) by (token_path, model) // token_path is coarse label from tracing
  - Postgres for canary diffs: select count(*) from canary_runs where result='slow' and run_ts > now() - interval '2 hours';

First-pass correlation matrix (what to check in parallel):
  - Client-side: SDK version, new retry config, payload size change.
  - Ingress: LB error spikes, connection resets, new IPs, increased TLS handshakes.
  - Serving runtime: queue depth, batching behavior, worker restart counts, kernel-level CPU steal.
  - Models: model size change, quantization profile change, tokenizer changes.
  - infra/cni/network: increased latency to NFS/remote cache, DNS spikes.
  - Dependencies: vector DB latencies, external APIs used in tool-calls.

Bisect-lite plan (use when suspecting recent code/config change):
  - Gather candidate commits / config releases (from deploy metadata, release tags).
  - Run a synthetic micro-benchmark across the commit-range in staging-dag: same seed prompts, fixed concurrency profile.
  - If reproduction in staging, binary search commits (script: infra/tools/commit-bisect.sh) until delta isolated.
  - If not reproducible, try canary split by traffic % and house-call deterministic inputs.

Canary comparison recipe (for behavioral regressions):
  1) Spin up canary model variant with identical infra that served the baseline.
  2) Replay 10k representative requests from the golden input set (store: s3://perf-golden-sets/chat/2024-08/). Capture per-request latency, token-level timelines, and stdout traces.
  3) For each request compute: latency_diff = canary.latency - baseline.latency; token_path_diff = diff(baseline.token_trace, canary.token_trace).
  4) Aggregate by prompt template and user-agent. Look for patterns with consistent positive latency_diff and matching token path divergence — those are highest priority.

Profiling checklist (when root cause not obvious):
  - CPU sampling: perf record on a stressed worker for 30s. Check top symbols, userspace kernels, and python GIL hotspots.
  - GPU profiling: use nvprof / Nsight on a dedicated node replicating the batch sizes from production. Look for kernels with abnormally high time in forward pass.
  - Allocation traces: track host memory allocations around request peaks (jemalloc stats) and check swap activity.
  - KV cache hit rates: check Redis/memcached latencies and miss ratios — cache churn leads to token regen and higher cost.
  - Trace sampling: enable 1:10 detailed traces and compare trace waterfall between baseline and regressed deploy.

Common root causes we've seen (war stories):
  - Subtle tokenizer change: new tokenization increases avg decode tokens by ~5-12% for a common template — manifests as higher token generation time and small p95 bump.
  - Batch scheduling regression: change in batch splitter caused more small batches under our steady load, increasing per-token overhead.
  - Kernel fallback: on newer CUDA driver, an optimized kernel fails and runtime falls back to slower generic kernel — shows up as host CPU + GPU idle but increased kernel duration.
  - External DB backpressure: a vector DB timing out caused request handlers to block, increasing queueing and perceived tail latency.

Mitigation decision tree (fast):
  - If rollback is trivial and regression large (>=20% p95 delta) -> rollback to previous deploy.
  - If narrow to one model variant -> route traffic away (runtime routing rule), scale up dedicated workers if capacity constrained.
  - If infra-induced (node-level) -> cordon node, drain, and trigger host replacement.
  - If external dependency -> circuit-breaker + fallback path (serve cached response or reduced token generation).

Data to capture in incident timeline (for postmortem):
  - symptom_timestamp, affected_routes, percent_of_traffic, mitigation_action, commit_id(s) involved, canary_run_ids, profiling_artifact_ids (s3 paths), owner and follow-ups.

Automation ideas / next runs:
  - Add a "token-path divergence" anomaly detector (baseline weekly traces -> compare windows).
  - Ship a lightweight synthetic runner that replays the golden set every hour across the fleet and records delta against last known baseline.
  - Add automatic commit-bisect trigger when canary/pipeline detects >=15% p95 increase between successive builds.

Useful tools & commands (copy/paste friendly):
  - Bisect script (staging): infra/tools/commit-bisect.sh --start v2024.08 --end HEAD --cases 200 --concurrency 8
  - Trace download: ./infra/tools/get-trace.sh <trace_id> --output traces/ && jq . traces/* | less
  - Local micro-bench: python perf/microbench/generate_fixed_seed.py --model redwood-open-8b --seed 20241003 --concurrency 12 --requests 1000

Notes to self (things we forgot last time):
  - Always pin the tokenizer version in model-bundles to avoid silent tokenization drift.
  - When profiling GPU kernels, ensure CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set to a single GPU to avoid sampling noise across multigpu nodes.
  - Document the canonical golden input sets and lock them (versioned S3 path).

Open action items (owners):
  - Janelle: add token-path divergence panel to the perf-triage dash (ETA 2024-11-15).
  - Ravi: wire commit metadata into alerts payload (so we know candidate commits in the first 2 min).
  - Tomas: prototype synthetic golden-set runner and store artifact IDs in canary runs.

Appendix — quick reproducibility checklist (for on-call):
  1) Reproduce locally with microbench and the failing deploy image.
  2) If repro, run quick perf record and capture /tmp/perf.data.
  3) If not repro, capture full trace sample from prod (increase sampling) and open a low-latency canary with 1% traffic and golden inputs.
  4) If bisecting, always validate candidate commit by running 3 full-run iterations to rule out noise.

If you find a new pattern that helped you find root cause, paste it here so future rotations can use it. — Marisol
